design_detail: Twenty-day residential laboratory study of oral methamphetamine self-administration in 8 volunteers, double-blind. On days 1, 5, 9, 13 and 17 participants received a sample capsule (0, 5 or 10 mg methamphetamine) and a sampled alternative of a $1 voucher; at the remaining dosing times that day and on the next two days they chose, on each of eight occasions, between the sampled capsule and the voucher. Active methamphetamine was available on days 5–7 and 13–15 and placebo on all other dosing days, with the order of the 5 mg and 10 mg conditions counterbalanced; days 1–3 were an acclimation period excluded from analysis. Outcomes were the number of drug choices, visual-analogue subjective ratings after the sample dose, psychomotor performance and continuously monitored food intake.
can_establish: That, under these conditions, adults with stimulant experience chose an oral methamphetamine capsule more often than placebo when a $1 voucher was the alternative, and that the sampled 10 mg dose produced larger positive subjective ratings than placebo while both active doses reduced measured daily food intake.
cannot_establish: A dose–response relation for self-administration (the two active doses did not differ); the role of the alternative's value (only $1 was used); the relation between subjective effects and drug taking in any quantitative way, because ratings were analysed only after the sample dose while choices were counted over three days; and anything about smoked, intranasal or injected use, about dependence, or about use outside a residential laboratory.

sample.recruitment: Word-of-mouth referral and newspaper advertisement in New York City; participants lived in a residential laboratory at the New York State Psychiatric Institute in groups of two or three (p. 76).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Healthy volunteers who passed medical and psychological evaluations and were within normal weight ranges; all reported previous stimulant use. The woman volunteer had a serum pregnancy test at screening and random urine pregnancy tests during the study (p. 76). No diagnostic criteria for stimulant use disorder are reported as inclusion criteria, and dependence status is not stated.
sample.demographics: 8 completers: 1 woman (Hispanic-American) and 7 men (3 Black-American, 3 White-American, 1 Hispanic-American), aged 23–42 years (mean 31.1), mean weight 71.5 kg (SD 13) (p. 76).
sample.attrition: Three other men began and did not complete: two for personal reasons unrelated to the protocol and one because he reported difficulty sleeping during the 10 mg phase (p. 76). The abstract and conclusions describe only the 8 completers.
sample.selection_effects: Volunteers recruited by advertisement and word of mouth who were willing to live in a laboratory for 20 days, mostly with cocaine rather than methamphetamine experience: only 3 of the 8 reported ever using methamphetamine before the study, and all received a 10 mg dose during pre-study training. Losing one participant because of a drug-related effect at the higher dose removes a person whose choices might have differed.

exposure.measurement: Drug administered in the laboratory: repackaged 5 mg methamphetamine hydrochloride tablets (a commercial product) in opaque capsules with lactose filler, or lactose alone for placebo, under double-blind conditions with capsule colour changing between conditions. Participants' own drug use was self-reported at screening; food intake was reported by bar-code scanner, acknowledged by staff, recorded by hand and validated against the daily trash (pp. 77).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: oral capsules containing 0, 5 or 10 mg of methamphetamine hydrochloride, available at 1000, 1400 and 1800 hours on three consecutive days per condition, with a maximum of eight choice occasions per condition; a 10 mg dose was also given once before the study for familiarization. The authors state the doses were chosen because they had produced dose-dependent subjective effects in an earlier study from the same laboratory (p. 77).
exposure.polysubstance: Self-reported at screening: 7 of 8 had used cocaine at least once and 3 had used methamphetamine at least once; 1 reported current cocaine use 4 times a week, 1 current cannabis use 4 times a week, 7 current alcohol use (1–15 drinks a week), 5 current tobacco use (7–20 cigarettes a day) and all 8 current caffeine use (2–30 cups a week). During the study tobacco was available under supervision except overnight; alcohol and other drugs were excluded by residence (p. 76).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Residential throughout the 20 days, so abstinence from non-study drugs other than tobacco and caffeine follows from the setting; no urine screening is reported. Each 3-day dose condition was separated by a day without any dose (p. 77).

comparison.controls: Placebo capsules in the same participants, in the 3-day condition that followed each active condition; the monetary alternative ($1 voucher) is the comparator within each choice.
comparison.matching: Within-person. The order of the two active doses was counterbalanced, but placebo conditions always occupied the same positions relative to the active ones (days 9–11 and 17–19), so the placebo comparison is not order-balanced.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable: each participant serves as his or her own control.

outcomes.instruments: Number of capsule choices over the eight choice occasions per condition; a 50-item visual analogue scale (0–100 mm) of mood and drug-effect items; a visual-analogue sleep questionnaire; a drug-effect questionnaire rating good effects, bad effects, drug strength and desire to take the drug again on 5-point scales and liking on a 9-point scale; a psychomotor battery (digit-symbol substitution, repeated acquisition, divided attention, rapid information processing, immediate and delayed digit recall); and continuous food-intake recording with calculation of total calories, macronutrient grams, number of eating occasions and intake per occasion (pp. 76–77).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard laboratory instruments with no external norms; food intake is measured rather than self-estimated, which is a strength.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Reinforcing effect' is operationalized as choosing the capsule over a $1 voucher more often than in the matched placebo condition; nothing is operationalized as harm.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Four planned pairwise comparisons were made for each outcome family, but the subjective battery alone has 50 items, of which 22 are tabulated for the 10 mg condition and 4 for the 5 mg condition, plus food-intake measures and six psychomotor tasks. The significance threshold was set at P<0.03 without justification (p. 77).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind administration; the outcomes are participant-generated (choices, ratings, food reports) and machine-recorded, so assessor blinding is less relevant, but blinding integrity was not tested.

analysis.effect_sizes: No effect sizes or confidence intervals are reported; F values appear in Tables 1 and 2 without degrees of freedom, and other results are given as means with P values. Mean number of drug choices out of eight: 4.3 (5 mg) against 1.4 in its placebo condition (P<0.02) and 4.4 (10 mg) against 1.3 (P<0.01), with no difference between the two active conditions or between the two placebo conditions. Peak subjective ratings after the 10 mg sample against its placebo (mean, SEM): good drug effect 36.42 (4.43) against 13.46 (0.96); high 26.30 (4.00) against 10.38 (1.34); stimulated 28.50 (6.38) against 4.38 (1.45); alert 59.50 (6.47) against 30.20 (5.52); hungry 11.46 (3.94) against 26.50 (7.18); sedated 3.54 (1.74) against 17.54 (2.24). After the 5 mg sample only four items differed: alert 59.40 (4.08) against 44.17 (2.58), energetic 34.25 (1.40) against 21.46 (3.03), talkative 46.46 (1.67) against 37.46 (2.99) and headache 5.13 (2.19) against 0.67 (0.15). Food intake fell by about 43% (5 mg) and about 37% (10 mg) relative to the matched placebo conditions (P<0.01), which the discussion converts to about 1415 kcal on average (Tables 1–2 and text, pp. 78–80).
analysis.covariates: None; repeated-measures ANOVA with planned comparisons, on data from the sample day for subjective and food-intake outcomes and across three days for choices.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Tables 1 and 2 list only the subjective items that reached significance, so the remaining items of the 50-item scale (including bad drug effect, anxious, irritable and paranoid-type items) cannot be evaluated; psychomotor results are dismissed in one sentence as showing no consistent effects and are not tabulated; food-intake values appear only in a figure.
analysis.power: Not reported; no sample-size calculation. With 8 participants and no confidence intervals, the absence of a dose difference in choice cannot be read as evidence of equivalence; the authors themselves offer two post-hoc explanations for it.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 8 residential volunteers, an oral methamphetamine capsule was chosen about 4.3–4.4 times out of 8 when active drug was available against 1.3–1.4 times in the matched placebo conditions; the 10 mg sample raised a range of positive subjective ratings and lowered hunger and sedation ratings, while the 5 mg sample moved only four items; both active doses cut measured daily food intake by roughly 37–43%; and self-administration did not increase from 5 mg to 10 mg.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that oral methamphetamine is a positive reinforcer in humans, and the discussion that the data are the first to show this under controlled conditions. In this sample and against a $1 alternative that is supported. Three qualifications the abstract does not carry: only 3 of the 8 participants reported ever having used methamphetamine before the study, so the sample is best described as stimulant-experienced rather than methamphetamine-experienced; the alternative reinforcer was a single $1 voucher per choice, and the authors' own argument that it was competitive rests on vouchers being chosen about 80% of the time under placebo; and the dissociation claimed between subjective and reinforcing effects compares ratings taken after one sample dose with choices counted over three days, which the authors acknowledge makes the relationship impossible to quantify.

timeline.event: Repeated oral methamphetamine administration in the same laboratory (Comer et al., 2001), the source of the dose selection and of comparable food-intake reductions of about 1150 and 1450 kcal; shares investigators and setting
Intranasal methamphetamine in the same research group: dose-related increases in positive subjective ratings and reduced hunger ratings, without a self-administration procedure

Intranasal self-administration against monetary alternatives of $5 and $20 in 13 men from the same group: drug chosen on 41% of occasions against $5 and 17% against $20, showing that the alternative's value matters

replication.where_it_stands: That methamphetamine functions as a reinforcer in human laboratory choice procedures is now supported by this study and by later work from the same laboratory using a different route and larger monetary alternatives; because the studies share investigators and setting they are not independent replications. The absence of a dose difference between 5 and 10 mg has not been resolved: the later intranasal work found drug choice to depend more on the size of the alternative than on the dose.

funding.funder: Grant DA-03746 (National Institute on Drug Abuse) (p. 80).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: the article carries no conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: Academic laboratory (New York State Psychiatric Institute and Columbia University). The study medication was a commercial methamphetamine product, repackaged by the institute pharmacy; no industry sponsorship is declared.

what_would_settle_it: A choice procedure with several monetary alternatives crossed with a wider dose range in the same participants, with subjective ratings taken at every choice rather than only after the sample dose, enough participants to estimate dose effects with intervals, and recruitment of people who actually use methamphetamine rather than stimulant-experienced volunteers in general.

domains.note: The order of the 5 mg and 10 mg conditions was counterbalanced across participants rather than randomized, and the placebo conditions always followed their matched active condition, so placebo is confounded with position in the study.

A drug-free day separated the 3-day conditions and days 1–3 were discarded as acclimation, but residual effects were found the morning after the 10 mg sample (more trouble sleeping and jitteriness), and the first three days of each condition contribute choices that may carry over.
Double-blind with matched capsules, but every participant had taken a 10 mg dose openly before the study and capsule colour changed with each condition; blinding integrity was not assessed.
Three of eleven who began did not complete, one of them because of difficulty sleeping during the 10 mg phase, which is a drug-related reason; only completers are analysed.
Choices and food intake are behavioural and machine-recorded, with the food records validated against the trash; subjective ratings are self-reports but that is the measure of interest.

Only the significant items of a 50-item scale are tabulated; psychomotor results are reported in one sentence without data; food-intake values appear only in a figure; F values are printed without degrees of freedom; the significance threshold is an unexplained P<0.03 and no protocol exists.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The core comparison (capsule chosen more often when it contained methamphetamine than when it did not) is behavioural, within person and double-blind, and is unlikely to be explained by these concerns. The overall rating is set by the reporting: a 50-item battery tabulated only where significant, undocumented degrees of freedom, a non-standard significance threshold and no protocol. The source can be cited for the demonstration that an oral methamphetamine capsule functions as a reinforcer against a $1 alternative in stimulant-experienced volunteers, for the subjective-effect profile of the sampled 10 mg dose against its placebo, and for the measured reduction in daily food intake; it cannot be cited for a dose–response relation, for the magnitude of reinforcement at other alternative values, or for a quantitative link between subjective effects and drug taking.

key_findings.finding: Capsule choice rose when the capsule contained methamphetamine: a mean of 4.3 of 8 choices in the 5 mg condition against 1.4 in its placebo condition (P<0.02) and 4.4 against 1.3 in the 10 mg condition (P<0.01), with no difference between the two active conditions or between the two placebo conditions.
key_findings.locator: Results › Reinforcing effects (p. 77, right column, continuing on p. 78); Figure 1 (p. 78)

key_findings.finding: Individual choices varied widely: in the 5 mg condition five participants chose the drug at least four times (range 4–8) and three chose it 0–2 times; in the 10 mg condition three chose it seven or eight times, three chose it four times and two chose it never.

The sampled 10 mg dose raised ratings of good drug effect (36.42, SEM 4.43, against 13.46, SEM 0.96), high (26.30 against 10.38), stimulated (28.50 against 4.38), alert (59.50 against 30.20), self-confident, social and talkative, and lowered ratings of hungry (11.46 against 26.50), sedated (3.54 against 17.54), sleepy, tired and depressed, all at P<0.03.

The sampled 5 mg dose changed only four of the fifty rated items against its placebo: alert (59.40 against 44.17), energetic (34.25 against 21.46), talkative (46.46 against 37.46) and headache (5.13 against 0.67).
No significant effects were found on the drug-effect questionnaire, including the items for drug strength and desire to take the drug again, in any condition.
key_findings.locator: Results › Subjective effects, last sentence of the 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The morning after the 10 mg sample day, participants reported more trouble sleeping and more jitteriness than after the matched placebo and after the 5 mg sample day (P<0.01); no other next-day differences were found.

Both active doses reduced measured total daily caloric intake relative to their placebo conditions, by about 43% (5 mg) and about 37% (10 mg) (P<0.01), with no significant difference between the two doses; intake of fat, carbohydrate and protein fell in parallel, so no macronutrient was selectively affected.
key_findings.note: The absolute intakes appear only in Figure 4; the Discussion states an average reduction of about 1415 kcal (p. 80).

key_findings.finding: The two doses reduced intake by different routes: at 5 mg through fewer eating occasions and longer intervals between them (both P<0.01), at 10 mg through a smaller mean intake per eating occasion (P<0.01).
key_findings.locator: Results › Food intake, last sentences (data reported as not shown)

key_findings.finding: Methamphetamine produced no consistent effects on the psychomotor battery, and those data are not reported.
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Data analysis (p. 77); Discussion, paragraph beginning 'Finally, methamphetamine produced little effect' (p. 80)

key_findings.finding: Vouchers were chosen on about half of the occasions when active methamphetamine was available and on about 80% of occasions under placebo, which the authors offer as evidence that the $1 alternative was a working reinforcer.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, paragraph beginning 'There are at least two possible explanations'

key_findings.finding: Only 3 of the 8 participants reported ever having used methamphetamine before the study, while 7 reported having used cocaine at least once; all received a single 10 mg methamphetamine dose during pre-study training.
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Participants (p. 76); Materials and methods › Procedure, 1st paragraph (p. 77)

reporting_issues.issue: The F values in Tables 1 and 2 are printed without degrees of freedom, and no degrees of freedom appear anywhere for the repeated-measures analyses; with 8 participants a planned pairwise within-person comparison would have 1 and 7 degrees of freedom.
reporting_issues.consequence: No test statistic in the paper can be checked against its sample size, and the P values cannot be recomputed.

reporting_issues.issue: The two active doses reduced caloric intake by about 43% (5 mg) and about 37% (10 mg), that is, the lower dose produced the larger reduction, while the Discussion gives a single average reduction of about 1415 kcal; the absolute intakes are only in Figure 4.
reporting_issues.consequence: The percentages and the kcal figure cannot be reconciled from the printed text, and the ordering of the two doses runs against the dose-ordering of the subjective effects; the figure would have to be digitized to check either.

reporting_issues.issue: The significance threshold is set at P<0.03 with no justification, and individual results are reported at P<0.01, P<0.02 and P<0.03.
reporting_issues.consequence: A non-standard, unexplained threshold applied across a 50-item rating battery and several behavioural outcomes, with no correction for multiplicity.

reporting_issues.issue: Three of the eleven people who began did not complete, one of them because of difficulty sleeping during the 10 mg phase, but the abstract and conclusions describe only the eight completers.
reporting_issues.consequence: A drug-related dropout is omitted from the paper's summary; the tolerability of the higher dose is better than it looks from the abstract.

reporting_issues.issue: Some standard errors in Table 1 are implausibly small for an 8-person sample on a 0–100 visual analogue scale, for example 'content' 30.80 with a standard error of 0.07 and 'dizzy' 0.00 with 0.00 under placebo.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either those placebo values were almost identical across all participants or the dispersion is mistyped; the corresponding F values (16.24 for 'content') cannot be checked without degrees of freedom.

reporting_issues.issue: Tables 1 and 2 list only the subjective items that reached significance, out of a 50-item scale that included bad drug effect, anxious, irritable and similar items.
reporting_issues.consequence: The absence of adverse subjective effects cannot be inferred from the tables, because unaffected and unreported items are indistinguishable.
